newsitem.title: USA: Alaska icon Iditarod celebrates quarter-century.
newsitem.headline: Alaska icon Iditarod celebrates quarter-century.

text.p: When a bunch of hardy Alaskans left Anchorage for the first Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race in 1973, big money was the last thing on their minds.
Now the annual 1,150-mile (1,850 km) race to Nome, which starts on Saturday, is an Alaska icon with a purse in excess of $400,000 and a budget running to millions of dollars.

The world's most famous sled-dog race opens its 25th edition with a ceremonial run from downtown Anchorage. The real competition begins on Sunday when dog teams leave from the nearby town of Willow -- a slight variation from the normal route forced by unusual snow conditions.
The race's fame has been a mixed blessing. Its heightened profile has inspired controveries including charges by animal welfare activists that the long race is too hard on the dogs.

Unseasonable warmth has made the trail slushy but a cold snap could turn it into a ribbon of slick ice, which defending champion Jeff King says could make the 1997 race a fast one. "My guess is, much to my dismay, I think we're going to have the potential for a real fast trail," he told the Alaska Public Radio Network.

In the past two years, winners reached Nome in nine days. It took Dick Wilmarth 20 days to win the first Iditarod, when 34 mushers competed for a $50,000 purse -- although when they set off race organisers did not have a dime in the bank.

The Iditarod is the annual highlight for professional mushers. Along with King, who also won in 1993, top contenders include two-time champion Martin Buser and 1995 champion Doug Swingley. Other potential winners are DeeDee Jonrowe, who is racing this year despite major injuries suffered in an auto wreck this winter, and former Yukon Quest International champions Bill Cotter and Charlie Boulding.

Race rookies include Spartanburg, South Carolina veterinarian Sonny King, who was inspired to get into the action after watching the race several times as part of the small medical army posted along the trail.
He said he wanted to see the Iditarod through musher's eyes this time. That meant frequent trips to Montana to train a dog team and long hours on a mountain bike and in a gym.
"I'm a 50-year-old veterinarian from the South. I've got to make sure I'm not the weak link in the team," he said during an orientation meeting for first-time racers.

Somewhere in the middle of the pack, probably, will be Joe Redington, the 80-year-old founder of the race who returns after a five-year hiatus. Although his hearing is fading, the octogenerian "Father of the Iditarod" is energetic and confident about his 23rd dog-sled trip along the route.
"I'm going to do the best that I can do. I'm going to have some fun, too," he said. "I'm not going to kill myself trying to get to Nome. I never have in the past."
